title: Known KPT changes in complete “I” sentences
summary: Apply familiar strong-to-weak KPT changes in short, complete A1 sentences with minä and a supplied context word.
objectives: Understand that minä means “I” and names the person doing the action.
Recognise the minä ending -n in a complete sentence.
Apply one previously learned strong-to-weak KPT change while every other sentence part is supplied.

sections.title: From a dictionary form to a complete sentence
paragraphs: A verb expresses an action or state. The dictionary form is the form listed in a dictionary, such as nukkua, meaning “to sleep”.
The minä form says that I perform the action. It ends in -n in these exercises, and the familiar KPT consonant becomes weak before that ending.
A short sentence can add one fixed context word after the verb. For example, hyvin means “well”. In Minä nukun hyvin, only nukun is formed; minä and hyvin are supplied unchanged.
keyPoints: Minä nukun hyvin. = I sleep well.

sections.title: One grammar decision at a time
paragraphs: This lesson uses only strong-to-weak changes already shown in the KPT recognition lesson: a double consonant shortens, k can disappear, p can become v, or a familiar cluster can weaken.
The time, place, or manner word is always shown with its English meaning. Copy it unchanged and focus only on the KPT verb form.
Verbs that need an object are left out here so the sentences do not require a new object-ending rule. Other verb types and strong-grade building are also left for later topics.

steps: Use the familiar weak change kk → k to make nuku-.
Place the supplied word hyvin (“well”) after the verb.
Start with lentää, meaning “to fly”, and the supplied stem lentä-.
The cluster nt weakens to nn: lennä-.
Place the supplied word tänään (“today”) after the verb.
The consonant p weakens to v: saavu-.
Place the supplied word pian (“soon”) after the verb.

commonMistakes: Do not simply attach -n to the complete dictionary form.
Change only the target verb; copy minä and the translated context word unchanged.
Do not add an object or another ending that the prompt does not ask for.
A long vowel or doubled consonant is meaningful; copy it accurately.

practiceExercises.prompt: Complete “I am sleeping now.” Minä ____ nyt. Use nukkua (“to sleep”); minä (“I”) and nyt (“now”) are supplied.
practiceExercises.explanation: The complete sentence Minä nukun nyt means “I am sleeping now”. In nukkua, kk weakens to k. Form nuku-, then add the minä ending -n: nukun.

parts.formation: Start with nukkua (“to sleep”). Change kk to k to make nuku-, then add the minä ending -n: nukun.

parts.formation: nyt is supplied as a complete fixed word meaning “now”. No ending rule is being tested.

practiceExercises.prompt: I am drawing here. Use piirtää (“to draw”) with the supplied words minä (“I”) and täällä (“here”).
practiceExercises.explanation: Minä piirrän täällä means “I am drawing here”. The dictionary form is piirtää. Its stem is piirtä-. Change rt to rr to make piirrä-, then add the minä ending -n: piirrän. Minä and täällä stay unchanged.

practiceExercises.prompt: Choose “I am arriving today.” Use saapua (“to arrive”); tänään means “today”.
practiceExercises.explanation: Minä saavun tänään means “I am arriving today”. In saapua, p weakens to v. Form saavu-, then add the minä ending -n: saavun.

Correct. In saapua, p weakens to v. Form saavu-, then add the minä ending -n: saavun.
“Saapun” keeps the strong p. In the minä form, p weakens to v: saavu- + n = saavun.
Saapua is the dictionary form “to arrive”. The sentence needs the minä form saavu- + n = saavun.

practiceExercises.prompt: Complete “I learn quickly.” Minä ____ nopeasti. Use oppia (“to learn”); minä (“I”) and nopeasti (“quickly”) are supplied.
practiceExercises.explanation: The complete sentence Minä opin nopeasti means “I learn quickly”. In oppia, pp weakens to p. Form opi-, then add the minä ending -n: opin.
